title: Gastrointestinal I: The Gut
summary: Disease of the esophagus, stomach and intestines.

lessons.title: Esophagus and GERD

levels.kid:
When you swallow, food slides down a stretchy tube called the esophagus to your stomach. At the bottom is a little door made of muscle. It opens to let food in, then shuts so stomach juice stays put.

Stomach juice is full of acid, which helps break down food. If the little door is loose, acid splashes back up. That burns, and people call it heartburn, even though it has nothing to do with the heart.

Eating smaller meals, not lying down right after eating, and some medicines that make less acid can help. If swallowing gets hard or hurts, a doctor should take a look with a tiny camera.
levels.hs:
The **esophagus** is a muscular tube that pushes food from the throat to the stomach by waves called **peristalsis**. At its lower end, the **lower esophageal sphincter (LES)** keeps stomach contents from flowing back.

**Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)** happens when acid repeatedly flows back up. Symptoms:
- **Heartburn**: burning behind the breastbone, often after meals or lying down
- **Regurgitation** of sour fluid
- Sometimes cough, hoarseness or sore throat
Risks include obesity, a **hiatal hernia** (part of the stomach slides above the diaphragm), pregnancy, smoking and large late meals.

**Treatment:** weight loss, raising the head of the bed, avoiding late meals, and medicines that reduce acid, especially **proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)**. Surgery that wraps the stomach around the LES (**fundoplication**) is an option for some.

**Complications:** inflamed esophagus (**esophagitis**), narrowing (stricture), and **Barrett's esophagus**, in which the lining changes type and carries a small risk of cancer.

**Alarm symptoms** need a camera test (endoscopy): trouble swallowing (**dysphagia**), weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools or anemia.

Other esophageal diseases: **achalasia**, in which the LES fails to relax, and **eosinophilic esophagitis**, an allergic inflammation that can make food stick.
levels.college:
**GERD pathophysiology:** mainly **transient LES relaxations** unrelated to swallowing, plus a hypotensive LES, hiatal hernia (loss of the crural diaphragm's pinch) and impaired clearance. Diagnosis is usually clinical with an empirical PPI trial; endoscopy for alarm features or failure; **ambulatory pH monitoring** proves reflux when endoscopy is normal.

**Barrett's esophagus:** replacement of squamous epithelium by columnar epithelium with **intestinal metaplasia** (goblet cells). Risk factors: chronic GERD, male sex, white ethnicity, central obesity, age over 50. It is the precursor of **esophageal adenocarcinoma** (lower third). Endoscopic surveillance with biopsies; dysplasia is treated with endoscopic resection and ablation.

**Esophageal cancer:** **squamous cell carcinoma** (upper and middle thirds; smoking, alcohol, hot beverages) vs **adenocarcinoma** (distal; GERD, obesity, Barrett's). Progressive dysphagia, first to solids then liquids, with weight loss.

**Dysphagia logic:**
- Solids only, progressive: mechanical (stricture, cancer).
- Solids and liquids from the start: motility disorder (**achalasia**: loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus, incomplete LES relaxation, aperistalsis; 'bird's beak' on barium swallow; diagnosed by manometry).
- Intermittent solid food impaction in a young atopic man: **eosinophilic esophagitis** (rings, furrows; eosinophils on biopsy).

**Tears:** **Mallory-Weiss** is a mucosal tear after forceful vomiting causing hematemesis; **Boerhaave syndrome** is a full-thickness rupture with chest pain, mediastinitis and subcutaneous emphysema, a surgical emergency.

PPIs irreversibly block the parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase and work best taken before a meal.
levels.phd:
The antireflux barrier is a dynamic system, not a valve. Most reflux events occur during **transient LES relaxations**, a vago-vagal reflex triggered by gastric distension of the proximal stomach, mediated through brainstem nuclei and inhibitory nitrergic neurons. This explains why large meals provoke reflux and why GABA-B agonists, which inhibit the reflex, were explored as therapy. After meals, an unbuffered **acid pocket** floats on top of the food at the gastroesophageal junction; a hiatal hernia traps it above the diaphragm, where it refluxes more easily.

The esophageal mucosal response is not simple acid burn. Animal and human studies suggest reflux triggers epithelial cytokine release (IL-8, IL-1β) and T-cell infiltration, with injury beginning in the submucosa, a cytokine-mediated model.

**Barrett's metaplasia** probably arises from progenitor cells at the gastroesophageal junction or transitional zone rather than transdifferentiation of squamous cells. Bile acids and acid induce **CDX2**, an intestinal transcription factor. Progression to adenocarcinoma involves early TP53 and CDKN2A alterations and genome doubling. Because most Barrett's patients never develop cancer, risk stratification (dysplasia, segment length, biomarkers) and non-endoscopic sampling devices are active research areas.

**Eosinophilic esophagitis** is a Th2-driven, food antigen-triggered disease. IL-13 induces eotaxin-3 from epithelial cells and downregulates barrier proteins; genetic risk loci include TSLP and CAPN14. Elimination diets, topical steroids and the IL-4 receptor alpha antibody dupilumab target this pathway.

**Achalasia** reflects selective loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons, possibly autoimmune after viral triggers in genetically susceptible people. Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) produces an identical picture. High-resolution manometry subtypes (Chicago classification types I-III) predict response, and **peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM)** emerged as an endoscopic alternative to surgical myotomy.
levels.expert:
**Chest pain is cardiac until proven otherwise.** Before calling it reflux, consider acute coronary syndrome, especially in older patients or those with risk factors; an ECG and troponin cost little.

**Typical GERD without alarm features:** lifestyle advice and a time-limited PPI trial is reasonable. **Endoscopy** is indicated for dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, GI bleeding or anemia, persistent vomiting, a palpable mass, new symptoms in older patients, or failure of PPIs, and for screening selected patients with multiple risk factors for Barrett's.

**PPI stewardship:** many patients stay on PPIs for years without a clear indication. Long-term use is associated with C. difficile infection, hypomagnesemia, reduced B12 absorption and fractures (associations, with variable causality). Step down to the lowest effective therapy or on-demand use when appropriate, but keep indicated therapy for severe esophagitis, Barrett's and high-risk NSAID users.

**Refractory 'reflux':** check adherence and timing (before meals). Then consider other diagnoses: eosinophilic esophagitis, achalasia, functional heartburn, rumination syndrome or gastroparesis. pH-impedance testing distinguishes true reflux from esophageal hypersensitivity.

**Emergencies:**
- **Food bolus impaction** with inability to swallow saliva needs urgent endoscopy; in young men think eosinophilic esophagitis and biopsy at the time.
- **Boerhaave:** vomiting followed by severe chest pain, fever and crepitus. CT with oral contrast; surgery or endoscopic intervention plus broad antibiotics. Delay greatly raises mortality.
- **Caustic ingestion:** no induced vomiting; early endoscopy grades injury.

**Achalasia is often misdiagnosed** as refractory GERD for years. A patient who regurgitates undigested food, has weight loss and dysphagia to liquids needs manometry. Before treating, exclude 'pseudoachalasia' from a tumor at the gastroesophageal junction, particularly in older patients with rapid weight loss.

keyPoints: The LES keeps stomach contents out of the esophagus; transient relaxations cause most reflux
GERD: heartburn and regurgitation; PPIs are first-line drug therapy
Alarm symptoms (dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, anemia) need endoscopy
Barrett's esophagus (intestinal metaplasia) is the precursor of adenocarcinoma
Achalasia: LES fails to relax; eosinophilic esophagitis: food impaction in young atopic patients

lessons.title: Stomach and Peptic Ulcer Disease

levels.kid:
Your stomach is a strong bag full of acid that helps break food into mush. To protect itself, it has a slimy coat, like a raincoat on the inside.

Sometimes the raincoat gets a hole and the acid makes a sore. That sore is called an ulcer. It can hurt in the top of the belly, like a burning or gnawing feeling.

Two big reasons for ulcers are a sneaky germ called H. pylori that lives in the stomach, and some pain medicines that weaken the raincoat.

Doctors can kill the germ with medicines and give other medicines that make less acid, so the sore can heal.
levels.hs:
The stomach makes **acid** and enzymes to digest food. Its lining protects itself with **mucus**, **bicarbonate** and good blood flow, supported by chemicals called **prostaglandins**.

**Peptic ulcer disease (PUD)** is a break in the lining of the stomach (**gastric ulcer**) or the first part of the small intestine (**duodenal ulcer**). Two main causes:
- **Helicobacter pylori**, a spiral bacterium that survives in the stomach and causes inflammation.
- **NSAIDs** (anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen and aspirin), which block prostaglandins and weaken the lining.
Smoking adds risk. Stress alone is a myth for most ulcers, except in severely ill hospital patients.

**Symptoms:** burning upper belly pain (**epigastric pain**), bloating, nausea. Classically, duodenal ulcer pain improves with food and gastric ulcer pain worsens with food, but this is unreliable.

**Complications:**
- **Bleeding**: vomiting blood or black, tarry stools (**melena**). The most common complication.
- **Perforation**: sudden severe pain and a rigid belly; air escapes under the diaphragm.
- **Obstruction** from scarring near the stomach outlet.

**Tests:** a **breath test** or stool test for H. pylori, and endoscopy when needed. **Treatment:** PPIs to heal the ulcer, a combination of antibiotics plus a PPI to clear H. pylori, and stopping NSAIDs. Barry Marshall and Robin Warren won a Nobel Prize for proving H. pylori causes ulcers.
levels.college:
**Acid secretion:** parietal cells secrete H+ through the H+/K+ ATPase in response to **gastrin** (from antral G cells), **histamine** (from enterochromaffin-like cells, H2 receptors) and **acetylcholine** (vagus, M3 receptors). **Somatostatin** from D cells inhibits. Mucosal defense depends on mucus-bicarbonate, epithelial renewal and blood flow, all supported by **COX-1-derived prostaglandins**.

**H. pylori:** urease converts urea to ammonia, buffering acid; flagella and adhesins allow mucus colonization; virulence factors include **CagA** and **VacA**. It infects roughly half the world. Outcomes depend on the pattern of gastritis:
- **Antral-predominant gastritis:** less somatostatin, more gastrin, high acid, **duodenal ulcer**.
- **Corpus-predominant (pangastritis):** atrophy, low acid, **gastric ulcer**, intestinal metaplasia and **gastric adenocarcinoma**; also **MALT lymphoma**, which can regress after eradication.

**Diagnosis:** urea breath test or stool antigen (stop PPIs about two weeks beforehand, since they cause false negatives); biopsy-based tests at endoscopy; serology cannot confirm cure. **Test of cure** after eradication is recommended. Eradication regimens (for example bismuth quadruple therapy) are chosen by local clarithromycin resistance.

**Gastric ulcers** need biopsy and often repeat endoscopy, because some are cancers. Duodenal ulcers are almost never malignant.

**Other causes:** **Zollinger-Ellison syndrome** (gastrin-secreting tumor; multiple or distal ulcers, diarrhea; association with MEN1); stress ulcers in critical illness (**Curling ulcer** after burns, **Cushing ulcer** after head injury, from vagal stimulation and acid hypersecretion).

**Complications:** bleeding (posterior duodenal ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery), perforation (anterior ulcers; free air on erect chest X-ray), and gastric outlet obstruction.
levels.phd:
The H. pylori story is a lesson in scientific skepticism. In the early 1980s, Warren noticed curved bacilli in gastritis biopsies and Marshall cultured them, an achievement partly due to an Easter weekend that left plates incubating longer than usual. The view that acid and stress caused ulcers was entrenched; Marshall famously drank a culture, developed gastritis and documented it. Eradication trials then showed ulcers stopped recurring, and the 2005 Nobel Prize followed.

Mechanistically, H. pylori is a master of niche adaptation. **Urease** generates an ammonia cloud; chemotaxis keeps bacteria in the near-neutral layer close to the epithelium. The **cag pathogenicity island** encodes a type IV secretion system that injects CagA into epithelial cells, where tyrosine phosphorylation by host kinases disrupts SHP-2 signaling, cell polarity and junctions, promoting proliferation and inflammation via NF-κB. **VacA** forms membrane channels and modulates T-cell responses. CagA was the first bacterial oncoprotein described, and H. pylori is classified as a group 1 carcinogen.

The **Correa cascade** describes stepwise progression: chronic active gastritis, multifocal atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia and intestinal-type adenocarcinoma. Eradication before atrophy reduces cancer risk most; after metaplasia, a 'point of no return' may limit benefit. Host polymorphisms (IL-1β, TNF) that increase inflammation and suppress acid raise cancer risk.

NSAIDs injure by two routes: topical (trapping of the weak acid inside epithelial cells, uncoupling mitochondria) and systemic COX-1 inhibition reducing protective prostaglandins. Selective COX-2 inhibitors reduced ulcer complications but revealed cardiovascular risk from imbalanced prostacyclin and thromboxane, a vivid example of mechanistic trade-off.

Rising clarithromycin and levofloxacin resistance has driven susceptibility-guided therapy and newer acid blockers, the potassium-competitive acid blockers, which suppress acid more consistently than PPIs.
levels.expert:
**Dyspepsia approach:** in younger patients without alarm features, **test and treat** for H. pylori is usually better than empirical endoscopy. Alarm features (bleeding, anemia, weight loss, progressive dysphagia, persistent vomiting, a mass, family history of gastric cancer, or onset at older age) call for endoscopy.

**Perforated ulcer:** sudden severe epigastric pain becoming generalized, a board-like abdomen and shoulder-tip pain. Erect chest X-ray shows free air in many cases, but CT is more sensitive. Resuscitate, give IV antibiotics and PPI, and get surgery involved; most need repair with an omental patch. Elderly and steroid-treated patients may have surprisingly few signs.

**Bleeding ulcer:** resuscitate first, then endoscopy. The **Forrest classification** grades rebleeding risk: active spurting, a non-bleeding visible vessel and adherent clot are high-risk stigmata needing endoscopic therapy and continued high-intensity PPI; a clean base is low risk. If endoscopy fails, interventional radiology embolization or surgery follows.

**After the ulcer:**
- Test for H. pylori in every ulcer patient; a biopsy taken during acute bleeding can be falsely negative, so retest later.
- Confirm eradication with a breath or stool test.
- Biopsy and re-scope gastric ulcers to document healing and exclude cancer.
- Stop NSAIDs where possible; if they are essential, add a PPI. Restart necessary antiplatelet therapy early after a bleed, since stopping it carries cardiovascular risk.

**When ulcers are refractory or atypical** (multiple, distal duodenal or jejunal, with diarrhea, or recurrent despite eradication and no NSAIDs), measure gastrin off PPIs and consider Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, hidden NSAID use, or Crohn's disease.

**Critical care:** stress ulcer prophylaxis is reserved for high-risk patients such as those on prolonged mechanical ventilation or with coagulopathy, and in neurosurgical patients after severe head injury.

keyPoints: Peptic ulcers occur in the stomach or duodenum
Main causes: H. pylori and NSAIDs (prostaglandin loss)
Complications: bleeding (most common), perforation, obstruction
H. pylori: breath or stool test; eradicate with antibiotics plus acid suppression; confirm cure
Gastric ulcers need biopsy to exclude cancer; think Zollinger-Ellison for refractory ulcers

lessons.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease

levels.kid:
Your intestines are long tubes that soak up food. Your body has a guard team, the immune system, that fights germs.

In inflammatory bowel disease, the guards get confused and attack the gut itself. The gut gets red and sore, like a scraped knee that will not heal.

People can get belly pain, lots of runny poo, sometimes with blood, and feel tired. They may lose weight because the sore gut cannot soak up food well.

There are two main kinds, called Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Doctors use medicines that calm the confused guards. It can come and go, and many people live full, busy lives.
levels.hs:
**Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)** is long-term inflammation of the gut caused by an overactive immune response in genetically prone people. It usually starts between ages 15 and 35, and it is different from irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), which has no inflammation.

Two main types:
- **Crohn's disease** can affect anywhere from **mouth to anus**, most often the end of the small intestine (**terminal ileum**). It comes in patches (**skip lesions**) and goes through the **whole thickness** of the bowel wall, so it can cause narrowings (**strictures**), abnormal tunnels (**fistulas**) and abscesses. Smoking makes it worse.
- **Ulcerative colitis (UC)** affects only the **colon**. It starts at the **rectum** and spreads upward without gaps, and it affects only the inner lining. The main symptom is **bloody diarrhea** with urgency.

Both can cause problems outside the gut: joint pain, eye inflammation, skin rashes and, in UC, a liver disease called primary sclerosing cholangitis. Children may grow poorly.

**Diagnosis:** blood tests, a stool test called **fecal calprotectin** (marks gut inflammation), and **colonoscopy** with biopsies. Stool cultures rule out infection.

**Treatment:** steroids calm flares but are not for long-term use. Long-term control uses drugs such as **mesalamine** (for UC), immune modifiers and **biologics**, antibodies that block specific inflammation signals. Surgery helps when medicine fails; removing the colon can cure UC.
levels.college:
**Crohn's disease:** transmural, discontinuous inflammation anywhere in the GI tract (ileocecal most often). Features: right lower quadrant pain, non-bloody diarrhea, weight loss, perianal disease (fistulas, abscesses, skin tags). Pathology: **non-caseating granulomas**, transmural lymphoid aggregates, 'cobblestone' mucosa, 'creeping fat'. Complications: strictures and obstruction ('string sign' on imaging), fistulas, abscesses, and malabsorption (B12 and bile acids after ileal disease; calcium oxalate stones; gallstones).

**Ulcerative colitis:** continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum proximally (proctitis, left-sided, extensive/pancolitis). Features: bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, urgency. Pathology: **crypt abscesses**, crypt distortion, pseudopolyps; loss of haustra ('lead pipe' colon). Complications: **toxic megacolon**, perforation, and colorectal cancer (risk rises with duration and extent). Strong association with **primary sclerosing cholangitis**.

**Extraintestinal manifestations:** peripheral arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis, episcleritis and uveitis, **erythema nodosum** and **pyoderma gangrenosum**, venous thromboembolism.

**Serology** (supportive only): ASCA tends toward Crohn's, p-ANCA toward UC.

**Treatment strategy:**
- 5-aminosalicylates for mild to moderate UC.
- Corticosteroids for induction only; budesonide for ileal Crohn's.
- Thiopurines and methotrexate as steroid-sparing agents.
- **Biologics:** anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab), anti-integrin (vedolizumab, gut-selective α4β7), anti-IL-12/23 or IL-23 (ustekinumab, risankizumab); oral small molecules (JAK inhibitors, S1P modulators).
- **Surgery:** colectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis can cure UC; Crohn's surgery is bowel-sparing (resections, strictureplasty) because disease recurs.

Smoking increases Crohn's risk and severity; quitting is a key intervention.
levels.phd:
IBD arises from a disrupted dialogue between the **mucosal immune system** and the **gut microbiota** in a genetically susceptible host, shaped by environment. The 2001 discovery of **NOD2** variants, an intracellular sensor of bacterial muramyl dipeptide, as the first Crohn's susceptibility gene reframed the disease as one of impaired innate handling of bacteria rather than pure over-activity. Genome-wide studies have since identified over 240 risk loci, many shared between Crohn's and UC, implicating autophagy (**ATG16L1**, IRGM), Paneth cell function, the **IL-23/Th17 axis** (IL23R), epithelial barrier genes and IL-10 signaling.

ATG16L1 risk variants impair Paneth cell granule secretion of antimicrobial peptides, linking autophagy, ER stress and defective bacterial clearance in the ileum. Very early onset IBD in infants can result from monogenic defects in **IL-10 or its receptor**, which are curable by hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, a striking proof that disordered immune regulation alone can cause colitis.

The microbiome in IBD shows reduced diversity, loss of butyrate-producing Firmicutes such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and expansion of Proteobacteria including adherent-invasive E. coli. Whether dysbiosis is cause or consequence remains debated; germ-free animal models generally fail to develop colitis, demonstrating that microbes are required.

Therapeutic progress follows immunology. Anti-TNF antibodies were the first transformative biologics. **Vedolizumab** exploits leukocyte trafficking biology: blocking α4β7 integrin binding to MAdCAM-1 on gut endothelium keeps lymphocytes out of the gut without the brain risk seen with the less selective natalizumab (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy). Anti-p19 antibodies targeting IL-23 specifically appear to outperform blockade of the shared p40 subunit.

The treatment goal has moved from symptom control to **mucosal healing** ('treat to target'), and histologic remission is increasingly studied as a deeper target.
levels.expert:
**Acute severe ulcerative colitis** is a medical emergency. The **Truelove and Witts criteria** flag it: at least six bloody stools daily plus systemic toxicity (tachycardia, fever, anemia, raised ESR or CRP). Admit, give intravenous corticosteroids, start **VTE prophylaxis** (IBD flares are prothrombotic; bleeding is not a contraindication), exclude **C. difficile and CMV**, and avoid opioids, anticholinergics and antidiarrheals, which can precipitate **toxic megacolon**. Daily abdominal X-ray if distension; colonic dilation with toxicity means surgical review. If there is no adequate response by about day three, start rescue therapy (infliximab or ciclosporin) or proceed to colectomy; delaying surgery raises mortality. Joint medical-surgical care is the standard.

**Before biologics or immunosuppression:** screen for latent tuberculosis, hepatitis B and C, HIV and varicella immunity, check thiopurine methyltransferase activity before thiopurines, and update non-live vaccines.

**Crohn's pitfalls:**
- New perianal pain with fever means abscess until proven otherwise: MRI pelvis and surgical drainage before escalating immunosuppression.
- A young person with chronic diarrhea, weight loss and raised calprotectin is not 'IBS'.
- Iron deficiency, B12 deficiency and bone loss are common and often missed.

**Long-term care:** surveillance colonoscopy for colorectal cancer starting about 8 years after onset of colitis (annually if PSC coexists); monitor growth and puberty in adolescents; address mental health, since anxiety and depression are common.

**Differentials that mimic IBD:** infectious colitis, ischemic colitis in older patients, NSAID enteropathy, celiac disease, intestinal tuberculosis (critical before starting anti-TNF in endemic areas), and lymphoma.

Shared decision-making matters: choosing between a biologic and surgery is a values conversation, not only a protocol.

keyPoints: IBD = Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis; immune-mediated, often begins at 15-35
Crohn's: mouth to anus, skip lesions, transmural, granulomas, fistulas and strictures
UC: rectum upward, continuous, mucosal, bloody diarrhea, toxic megacolon, PSC
Fecal calprotectin and colonoscopy with biopsy diagnose it
Steroids for flares only; biologics and immunomodulators maintain remission; colectomy cures UC

lessons.title: GI Bleeding

levels.kid:
Sometimes the long food tube inside you starts to bleed, like a scrape on the inside.

If the bleeding is high up, near the stomach, a person might throw up blood, or their poo might turn black and sticky like tar. If it is low down, near the end, the poo may have bright red blood.

Losing a lot of blood can make someone pale, dizzy and weak, because blood carries oxygen.

Doctors act fast. They give fluids and sometimes blood through a tube in the arm. Then they look inside with a tiny camera on a long bendy tube, find the bleeding spot and stop it.
levels.hs:
**Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding** is divided by where it starts:
- **Upper GI bleeding:** from the esophagus, stomach or duodenum. Signs: vomiting blood (**hematemesis**), 'coffee-ground' vomit (blood altered by acid) and **melena** (black, tarry, smelly stool).
- **Lower GI bleeding:** from the colon or rectum. Sign: **hematochezia**, bright red or maroon blood from the rectum. A very fast upper bleed can also cause red blood from below.

**Common causes:**
- Upper: **peptic ulcers** (most common), **esophageal varices** (swollen veins from liver cirrhosis), **Mallory-Weiss tears** after vomiting, inflamed esophagus or stomach, and cancer.
- Lower: **diverticular bleeding** (painless, in older adults), **angiodysplasia** (fragile vessels), colitis, colorectal cancer and **hemorrhoids**.

**How doctors judge severity:** fast heart rate, low blood pressure, dizziness on standing, fainting, and blood tests showing low hemoglobin. Blood thinners make bleeding worse.

**Treatment steps:**
- **Resuscitate first:** two large IV lines, fluids, and blood transfusion if needed.
- Give acid-reducing medicine for suspected ulcer bleeding.
- **Endoscopy** for upper bleeding or **colonoscopy** for lower bleeding to find and stop the source with clips, heat or injections.
- If those fail: a CT angiogram to locate the bleed, and a radiologist can block the vessel (**embolization**), or surgery.
levels.college:
**Definitions:** upper GI bleeding originates proximal to the **ligament of Treitz** (duodenojejunal flexure). Urea rises disproportionately in upper bleeds because digested blood protein is absorbed.

**Upper GI bleed causes:** peptic ulcer (H. pylori, NSAIDs, antiplatelets), **variceal hemorrhage** (portal hypertension), erosive esophagitis or gastritis, Mallory-Weiss tear, malignancy, Dieulafoy lesion (an aberrant submucosal artery) and aortoenteric fistula after aortic graft surgery.

**Lower GI bleed causes:** diverticulosis (arterial bleeding at the neck of a diverticulum, painless, often right colon), angiodysplasia (associated with aortic stenosis via acquired von Willebrand deficiency, Heyde syndrome), ischemic colitis (painful), IBD, infectious colitis, neoplasia, post-polypectomy bleeding, hemorrhoids. In children, **Meckel's diverticulum** with ectopic gastric mucosa is a classic cause of painless bleeding.

**Risk scores:** the **Glasgow-Blatchford score** (urea, hemoglobin, systolic pressure, pulse, melena, syncope, liver disease, heart failure) identifies very low-risk patients suitable for outpatient care; the Rockall score adds endoscopic findings to predict death and rebleeding.

**Management principles:**
- Restrictive transfusion: a hemoglobin threshold of about 70 g/L (higher in cardiovascular disease) improves outcomes in most patients.
- Correct coagulopathy and consider reversal of anticoagulants in major bleeding.
- IV PPI before endoscopy in suspected non-variceal bleeding; endoscopy within 24 hours.
- **Suspected variceal bleed:** vasoactive drugs (terlipressin or octreotide), **prophylactic antibiotics** (reduce infection, rebleeding and death in cirrhosis), endoscopic **band ligation**; balloon tamponade as a bridge; **TIPS** for refractory or high-risk bleeding.
- **Lower GI bleed:** colonoscopy after bowel preparation; CT angiography first if unstable, followed by catheter embolization.
levels.phd:
Several modern principles of GI bleeding management come from trials that overturned intuition. The 2013 Villanueva trial randomized upper GI bleeding patients to transfusion at a hemoglobin threshold of 70 versus 90 g/L; the restrictive strategy reduced mortality and rebleeding, especially in cirrhosis with Child-Pugh A and B. The mechanism is plausibly hemodynamic: aggressive volume and blood replacement raises portal pressure and may dislodge clots, a reminder that 'normalizing numbers' can harm.

The **HALT-IT** trial (about 12,000 patients) found that tranexamic acid did not reduce death from GI bleeding and increased venous thromboembolic events, so it is not routinely recommended, unlike in trauma or postpartum hemorrhage, where timing and fibrinolytic biology differ.

Variceal rupture follows physics. Wall tension, by Laplace's law, increases with transmural pressure and vessel radius and decreases with wall thickness; large varices with thin walls (red wale signs) under a hepatic venous pressure gradient above about 12 mmHg are the ones that bleed. Non-selective beta blockers lower portal pressure by reducing cardiac output (β1) and causing splanchnic vasoconstriction via unopposed α-tone (β2 blockade). **Pre-emptive TIPS** in high-risk patients (Child-Pugh C or B with active bleeding) improved survival in randomized studies, illustrating risk-stratified escalation.

In peptic ulcer hemorrhage, sustained high gastric pH is mechanistically important: platelet aggregation and clot stability are impaired below about pH 6, and pepsin dissolves clots in acid, which is the rationale for intensive PPI therapy after endoscopic hemostasis. Endoscopic hemostasis has expanded from injection and thermal coagulation to over-the-scope clips and topical hemostatic powders. Doppler endoscopic probes that detect residual arterial flow beneath an ulcer stigma may predict rebleeding better than visual Forrest grading alone.
levels.expert:
**The first ten minutes:** airway (protect it in massive hematemesis or altered consciousness, especially before endoscopy for varices), two large-bore cannulas, blood for group and crossmatch, hemoglobin, coagulation, urea and lactate, and activate the major hemorrhage protocol if the patient is unstable. A normal first hemoglobin does not exclude major bleeding, because concentration falls only after hemodilution.

**Read the clues:**
- Liver disease stigmata (jaundice, ascites, spider angiomas) mean treat as variceal until endoscopy: start vasoactive therapy and antibiotics immediately.
- A high urea-to-creatinine ratio supports an upper source.
- Bright red rectal bleeding with shock should prompt an upper endoscopy, because about one in ten such cases comes from a brisk upper source.
- Prior aortic graft plus a 'herald' bleed: think aortoenteric fistula and get a CT angiogram now.

**Antithrombotic decisions** are a balance. Warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants may need reversal agents in life-threatening bleeding; aspirin for secondary prevention should usually be resumed soon after hemostasis, because stopping it increases cardiovascular death. Discuss dual antiplatelet therapy after a recent stent with cardiology rather than stopping both drugs.

**Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0 or 1:** many such patients can be managed as outpatients with early endoscopy, saving admissions safely.

**After hemostasis:** test for H. pylori, stop NSAIDs, decide on PPI duration, and in variceal bleeding start secondary prophylaxis (beta blocker plus repeated banding) and evaluate for transplant. A variceal bleed in cirrhosis marks decompensation and sharply worsens prognosis.

**Occult bleeding** presenting as iron deficiency anemia in an adult man or post-menopausal woman requires both upper endoscopy and colonoscopy to exclude cancer; 'just give iron' is a classic error.

keyPoints: Upper GI bleed (above the ligament of Treitz): hematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, melena
Lower GI bleed: hematochezia; diverticula, angiodysplasia, colitis, cancer, hemorrhoids
Peptic ulcer is the commonest upper source; varices in cirrhosis are the most lethal
Resuscitate first; restrictive transfusion; endoscopy within 24 hours
Variceal bleed: vasoactive drug, antibiotics, band ligation, TIPS if needed

lessons.title: The Acute Abdomen

levels.kid:
Sometimes a tummy ache is just gas or a bit of a bug. But sometimes a very bad, sudden belly pain means something inside needs a doctor right away. Doctors call this an acute abdomen.

One example is appendicitis. The appendix is a tiny finger-shaped pouch on your gut. If it gets blocked and swollen, the pain often starts around the belly button, then moves to the lower right side. Walking, coughing or bumps in the car hurt.

Doctors gently press on the belly, ask lots of questions and may take pictures with scans. Some problems need medicine, and some need a surgeon to fix them.
levels.hs:
An **acute abdomen** is sudden, severe abdominal pain that may need urgent surgery. The key job is to spot the patients who are seriously ill.

**Where it hurts helps:**
- **Right lower quadrant:** **appendicitis** (pain starts near the belly button, moves to the right lower side, with loss of appetite, nausea and fever).
- **Right upper quadrant:** gallbladder inflammation (**cholecystitis**).
- **Upper middle, through to the back:** **pancreatitis**.
- **Left lower quadrant:** **diverticulitis** in older adults.
- **Everywhere, colicky, with vomiting and a swollen belly:** **bowel obstruction**.
- Sudden severe pain everywhere with a rigid belly: **perforation** of the gut.

**Peritonitis** means the lining of the abdomen is inflamed. Signs: the patient lies very still, the belly is hard (**guarding** and **rigidity**), and letting go after pressing hurts (**rebound tenderness**).

**Don't forget:** in anyone who could be pregnant, a pregnancy test is essential (**ectopic pregnancy** can bleed dangerously). Testicular torsion, heart attacks, pneumonia and diabetic ketoacidosis can also cause belly pain.

**Tests:** blood tests, urine test, pregnancy test, ultrasound, and **CT scan** in many adults. Treatment depends on the cause: fluids, pain relief, antibiotics, and surgery when needed. Giving pain relief does not hide the diagnosis, so patients should not be left in pain.
levels.college:
**Pain physiology shapes the history.** Visceral pain is dull, poorly localized and felt in the midline according to embryology: foregut (stomach to mid-duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas) in the epigastrium, midgut (to the distal transverse colon, including the appendix) around the umbilicus, hindgut in the suprapubic region. When inflammation reaches the **parietal peritoneum**, somatic nerves localize pain sharply. This explains the migration of appendicitis pain to **McBurney's point**. Referred pain follows shared dermatomes: diaphragmatic irritation refers to the shoulder (**Kehr's sign** in splenic rupture).

**Key conditions:**
- **Appendicitis:** luminal obstruction (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia); Rovsing's, psoas and obturator signs; Alvarado and similar scores; ultrasound in children and pregnancy, CT in adults.
- **Small bowel obstruction:** adhesions (most common in those with prior surgery), hernias, Crohn's; colicky pain, vomiting, distension, obstipation; dilated loops with air-fluid levels.
- **Large bowel obstruction:** colorectal cancer, **volvulus** (sigmoid 'coffee bean' sign), diverticular stricture; a competent ileocecal valve creates a closed loop at risk of cecal perforation.
- **Acute mesenteric ischemia:** embolus (often atrial fibrillation), arterial thrombosis, venous thrombosis or non-occlusive ischemia; **pain out of proportion to examination**; lactate rises late; CT angiography.
- **Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm:** pain to the back, hypotension, pulsatile mass.
- **Ectopic pregnancy:** amenorrhea, pain, vaginal bleeding, positive beta-hCG.
- **Perforated viscus**, **diverticulitis**, **cholecystitis**, **pancreatitis**.

**Medical mimics:** inferior myocardial infarction, lower lobe pneumonia, diabetic ketoacidosis, sickle cell crisis, adrenal crisis, hypercalcemia, porphyria.

**Atypical presentations:** older adults, immunosuppressed patients and those on steroids may have few signs and a normal white cell count despite catastrophe.
levels.phd:
The acute abdomen illustrates how diagnostic reasoning interacts with probability and harm. Clinical scores (Alvarado, the Appendicitis Inflammatory Response score, the Adult Appendicitis Score) improve on gestalt mainly at the extremes: they can rule out or rule in, but intermediate scores are best served by imaging. The negative appendectomy rate, once accepted at 15 to 20%, has fallen markedly with routine CT in adults, at the cost of radiation exposure and incidental findings, a trade-off that drives ultrasound-first and low-dose CT strategies, especially in the young.

The classic teaching that appendicitis inevitably progresses to perforation has been challenged. Epidemiological data suggest uncomplicated and complicated appendicitis may be partly distinct diseases, and randomized trials (APPAC in Finland, CODA in the United States) showed that antibiotics alone treat many uncomplicated cases, although a meaningful fraction later undergo appendectomy, and an appendicolith predicts failure and complications. This reframes treatment as a shared decision rather than reflex surgery.

The old dogma that analgesia masks peritonitis has been tested in randomized trials and systematic reviews: opioid analgesia does not reduce diagnostic accuracy and improves comfort. The myth persisted for nearly a century, attributed to early twentieth-century surgical texts.

Mesenteric ischemia exposes the limits of laboratory tests. Lactate reflects global hypoperfusion and liver clearance; it can be normal early while the bowel is dying, and intestinal fatty acid binding protein and D-lactate have not achieved reliable diagnostic accuracy. Mortality remains high, and the main lever is clinical suspicion leading to early CT angiography.

Bowel obstruction physiology involves fluid sequestration, bacterial translocation and rising intraluminal pressure that eventually exceeds venous then arterial pressure, causing strangulation. Water-soluble contrast challenges in adhesive small bowel obstruction are both diagnostic and possibly therapeutic, reducing surgery and length of stay.
levels.expert:
**Your first question is not 'what is it' but 'how sick is this patient'.** Vital signs, mental state, lactate and the abdomen's tone decide whether you resuscitate first and think later. Septic or hypotensive patients get fluids, cultures, broad antibiotics and early senior surgical review in parallel with diagnosis.

**A focused system:**
- Exact onset: sudden (perforation, rupture, torsion, mesenteric embolus) versus gradual (inflammation).
- Character: colicky (obstruction, stones) versus constant (inflammation, ischemia).
- Always: pregnancy test where possible, ECG in older patients, urinalysis, glucose, lipase, and a genital examination in boys and men with lower abdominal pain, because testicular torsion often presents as abdominal pain in adolescents.
- Examine hernial orifices: a small incarcerated femoral hernia in an older woman is a classic missed cause of obstruction.

**Red flags demanding immediate action:**
- Pain out of proportion to signs, especially with atrial fibrillation: CT angiography for mesenteric ischemia.
- Older patient with 'renal colic' and hypotension: ruptured aortic aneurysm until proven otherwise; permissive hypotension and direct transfer to the vascular team.
- Positive pregnancy test with pain: ectopic until the location of the pregnancy is proven.
- Peritonism with free air: perforation; resuscitate, antibiotics, operate.

**Pitfalls:**
- A normal white count does not exclude appendicitis or ischemia.
- Elderly, diabetic, immunosuppressed and steroid-treated patients hide peritonitis.
- Diagnosing 'gastroenteritis' without diarrhea is a classic trap; vomiting and abdominal pain alone may be obstruction or appendicitis.
- Children: intussusception, malrotation with volvulus (bilious vomiting in an infant is a surgical emergency), and diabetic ketoacidosis.

**Re-examine.** Serial examination by the same clinician over hours is one of the most powerful diagnostic tests, and 'discharge with safety-net advice' must include clear reasons to return.

keyPoints: Acute abdomen = sudden severe abdominal pain that may need urgent surgery
Location guides the differential: RLQ appendicitis, RUQ cholecystitis, LLQ diverticulitis, epigastric to back pancreatitis
Peritonitis: guarding, rigidity, rebound; free air means perforation
Always pregnancy test; think AAA, mesenteric ischemia, MI, DKA and testicular torsion
Analgesia does not mask the diagnosis; resuscitate the unstable patient first
